cards.title: Approximation tradeoff for Set Cover below exhaustive search
cards.formal: Determine the best approximation ratio for parameterized Set Cover achievable in time n^{k−ε}, where ε is a positive constant and k refers to the solution-size parameter. The missing exponent in the extraction is k−ε, and n counts all vertices of the bipartite set–element incidence graph. The source contrasts its known logarithmic-power hardness with a polynomial-time logarithmic approximation and asks for the intervening tradeoff. A completed benchmark still needs the precise parameter/promise convention, allowable f(k) multiplier, asymptotic precision and lower-bound hypothesis stated below; this card does not silently choose them.
cards.why: The intended curve would describe how approximation quality changes when an algorithm can spend nearly the time needed for exhaustive parameterized search, a basic unresolved tradeoff for a central covering problem.
cards.status_note: Read the source’s instance and approximation definitions, exact Theorem 1 threshold, conclusion and April 2019 full revision. The 9 September 2026 paper confirms that substantial Set Cover approximation gaps remain. That evidence does not fix every parameter and acceptance convention for this broad optimal-tradeoff question; these are recorded as the remaining formulation issue.

sentences: Set Cover seeks the fewest set vertices covering all element vertices in an explicit incidence graph.
The source asks for the optimal approximation ratio in time n^{k−ε}, with a fixed positive exponent saving.
Known conditional lower bounds leave a gap below the polynomial-time logarithmic approximation.
A September 2026 follow-up still describes that gap, while obtaining results for related monotone-circuit problems.

cards.definitions: An instance is a finite bipartite graph I=(S⊔U,E), with one vertex for each available set in S and each universe element in U. An edge (s,u) means set s contains u. All vertices, sides and incidences are explicit; n=|S|+|U|, not just |U| or the number of encoded bits. For nonempty U with every element incident to some set, OPT(I)=min{|C|:C⊆S and every u∈U has a neighbor in C}. A cover is an explicit subset C, and its ordinary multiplicative approximation ratio is |C|/OPT(I). Empty or uncoverable instances can be recognized separately; the meaningful ratio regime has 1≤OPT(I)≤|S|. In the source’s ordinary approximation definition, an algorithm must return a valid cover with |C|≤r·OPT(I) on every coverable input. Its parameterized lower bounds instead take an integer target k and distinguish OPT(I)≤k from OPT(I)>h for an absolute threshold h>k, leaving the middle range unrestricted. That promise gap corresponds to a multiplicative scale h/k, not h itself. The theorem permits running time f(k)n^{k−ε} for an arbitrary computable function f, whereas the concluding question displays n^{k−ε}. The choice between actual-optimum-dependent running time and a supplied target with a promise has to be recorded explicitly before optimizing a ratio. The intended time improvement uses fixed ε>0, independent of n; it is not a saving that vanishes as n grows. It is also different from n^{o(k)} or fixed-parameter time f(k)n^c with c independent of k. The source’s SETH is the deterministic Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis: for every η>0 there is an integer clause width q such that q-CNF satisfiability on N variables has no deterministic O(2^{(1−η)N}poly(M))-time algorithm, where M is the explicit formula size. This is a hypothesis used for the cited lower bound, not a proven fact or an automatically chosen hypothesis for the unfinished optimality target. Natural logarithms are used in the displayed approximation scales, and logarithmic asymptotics concern sufficiently large n.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify the exact solution-size promise, input and running-time model, permitted parameter factors and asymptotic comparison of approximation ratios. Then characterize the achievable ratio with matching upper and lower bounds at that precision, with every conditional lower-bound assumption explicit. A single improved factor, a hardness result in a different time regime, or the unspecified nearby function (ln n)^{1/ρ(k)} is not the requested full tradeoff. The statement remains incomplete until those source-supported conventions are fixed.

cards.title: Inseparable degree in algebraic-independence testing
cards.formal: The source asks whether dependence on inseparable degree is essential in testing algebraic independence over positive-characteristic fields. It contrasts a randomized criterion-based test whose cost depends on that parameter with already-known AM∩coAM decision protocols that have no such promise. This is a research direction, not yet one quantified algorithmic proposition: the source does not say whether the desired advance is a faster ordinary test, a new criterion, or removal of the promise from its restricted faithful-homomorphism construction. The exact target and resource bound remain to be specified.
cards.why: The direction concerns a basic obstruction to extending algebraic-independence methods to small characteristic, but its scientific content depends on separating ordinary algorithms, interactive verification and explicit rank-preserving constructions.
cards.status_note: Read the field-theory definitions in the December 2022 full revision, the criterion theorem and the finite-field interactive result. A May 2025 TIFR seminar still describes the ordinary finite-field testing problem as open. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no source that turns this qualitative direction into the specific benchmark target requested by the card. No general new algorithmic conjecture is invented.

sentences: Algebraic independence means that no nonzero polynomial relation holds among the input polynomials.
In small characteristic, the source uses a Frobenius-power inseparability parameter in its criterion and restricted faithful-map construction.
That parameter is not the conventional inseparable extension degree.
Interactive AM∩coAM verification already avoids the parameter promise, but does not give an ordinary randomized polynomial-time algorithm.
The source does not select which stronger test or construction should lose its dependence, so an exact new target remains to be specified.

cards.definitions: For a field F of characteristic p>0 and polynomials f₁,…,f_m∈F[x₁,…,x_n], algebraic independence over F means that no nonzero A∈F[z₁,…,z_m] satisfies A(f₁,…,f_m)=0. Their algebraic rank k is the maximum size of an independent subfamily; equivalently k=trdeg_F F(f₁,…,f_m), where F(f) denotes the field generated by these polynomials and F. An algebraic element is separable if its irreducible minimal polynomial has no repeated root. For a finite algebraic extension K/L in characteristic p, write Sep(K/L) for the elements of K separable over L. The source’s parameter t(K/L) is the least p-power p^e, e≥0, such that every a∈K has a^{p^e}∈Sep(K/L). It is one for a separable extension. This is generally different from the conventional inseparable degree [K:Sep(K/L)]; for example F_p(x,y)/F_p(x^p,y^p) has source parameter p and conventional degree p². For a polynomial family f of rank k, consider coordinate sets S⊆[n] of size n−k such that x_S is algebraically independent over F(f). Then F(x)/F(f,x_S) is finite algebraic. Define t(f) as the minimum of t(F(x)/F(f,x_S)) over such S. This is the coordinate-completion convention in full-version Definition 2.6; such sets exist by extending a transcendence basis with coordinates. An F-algebra homomorphism Φ on F[x] is faithful for f if trdeg_F F(Φ(f₁),…,Φ(f_m))=k. Preserving rank over F and preserving it over a larger coefficient field are distinct statements. The source’s deterministic construction concerns sparse polynomials and certain products of variable-disjoint multilinear sparse polynomials under constant k and t. A sparse representation lists nonzero monomials and coefficients; a circuit representation is an arithmetic directed acyclic graph and may succinctly represent exponentially large degree. The broader randomized independence theorem concerns circuit inputs over finite fields and has time polynomial in s and binomial(n+t,n), where s is the input size and t is a promised bound in the independent case. AM denotes languages with polynomial-size, constant-round public-coin interactive proofs, with completeness at least 2/3 and soundness at most 1/3; coAM comprises complements of AM languages. Membership in both classes gives separate protocols for the two answers, not a randomized polynomial-time decision algorithm without a prover. A particular finite-field encoding, resource model and desired bound are not selected for the open direction.
cards.answer_criterion: Recover a single source-supported claim with explicit input representation and parameters, a specified algorithmic or algebraic output, allowed randomness or interaction, and an exact resource or structural improvement. Then prove or refute that claim. Restating the existing AM∩coAM result, or removing the parameter from an unrelated theorem, does not answer an unspecified new improvement. This card is not certified as a completed open benchmark until that target is fixed.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
